metadata.title: Michael Burry Says He’s Shorting The Market’s ‘Generals’ As Apple Flashes A Warning Last Seen In 2002

content.text:
He named Apple as a possible target and separately disclosed a bet against private equity.
Burry bought Nvidia calls before Monday's rally, exited his semiconductor ETF puts and later sold his remaining Nasdaq 100 puts.
He also attributed Wednesday's Nasdaq 100 bounce to buyers returning near 25,000.
"The Big Short" investor Michael Burry said that puts on his preferred targets had grown expensive, prompting him to look for his next bearish bet among the stocks still holding up. On Wednesday, he said he was shorting the market's "generals" after pointing to Apple as a possible target.
"I am shorting generals today will put in a trading post," the "Big Short" investor said in his Cassandra Unchained Substack chat. Separately, Burry also said he was betting against private equity. He did not name a private equity firm or say whether he had opened an Apple (AAPL) position as yet.
Burry flagged Apple's resilience in a note by BTIG chief market technician Jonathan Krinsky. On Friday, Apple closed within 5% of its 52-week high, while the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ), which tracks the Nasdaq 100, was at least 19% below its own 52-week high. Krinsky said that combination was last seen in May 2002.
Burry Looks For His Next Short Among Stocks Still Holding Up
"I am still bearish but I know we do not usually go straight down, and we have come down a good amount," Burry said. "For me, the problem is puts have become expensive in my targeted securities."
A put gives its buyer the right to sell a stock at a set price. The higher the upfront cost, the further the stock has to fall for the bet to pay off at expiration. That cost made Burry take another look at the stocks investors had held on to through the selloff.
Burry had already scaled back his broader bets against tech. Before Monday's rally, he bought Nvidia (NVDA) calls and sold his remaining puts on the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH). In a Wednesday portfolio update, he said he had also sold the remaining half of his Nasdaq 100 puts and held about 25% in cash. Aside from puts on Palantir (PLTR) and MetLife (MET), he called his portfolio at the time almost entirely long.
Burry Credits 25,000 For Nasdaq 100 Bounce
Burry traced Wednesday's Nasdaq 100 rebound to a familiar level. The index had slipped below 25,000 on Friday before closing back above it. When it returned to that round number Wednesday, Burry said buyers stepped in again.
"Barron's called asking me if I was the one who caused it because CNBC said I was long around the time that bounce happened. I highly doubt it," he said.
On Hong Kong tech, Burry said the selling had gone on so long it felt like the new normal. When asked about persistently heavy trading in JD.com (JD), one of his largest holdings, he said he watches how often the shares change hands. "I look at it primarily for stock ownership turnover, which is irrespective of dollar volume," he said.
What Happened To Apple After May 2002?
Apple lost half its value between May and August 2002. Krinsky cautioned against using the decline as a forecast for today's Apple, but he saw a risk in how far it had pulled ahead of other tech stocks.
"With that said, it does show just how extreme the divergence has become and at the end of the day, it's still a technology stock and thus we think it remains increasingly vulnerable to 'catching down' to the rest of the tape," Krinsky said. Apple held its ground on Wednesday, rising 0.4% to $355.58 for its third straight gaining session.
Monday's Nasdaq 100 rebound also gave Krinsky pause. The index jumped at least 5% after falling at least 5% on Friday. To Krinsky, that left "plenty of room for markets to work lower over the coming weeks before we get a full-fledged washout."
Why Apple Is A Rare Short For Burry
"The generals are still standing," Burry said just days earlier on Monday. He counted Apple (AAPL), Costco (COST) and Walmart (WMT) among the stocks investors hold on to early in a selloff, even when their prices look steep relative to their growth. By the end of last week, the Nasdaq 100 fell 10% and the S&P 500 lost 9%. Apple fell 4%, while Costco slipped just 0.4% and Walmart gave up only 0.1%.
Their staying power makes a short hard to time. By Burry's count, the market's leaders held up for six months after the 2000 peak and seven to eight months after the 2007 peak. When asked in August about betting against Apple, he said, "It is like Costco. Once in a blue moon I take my chances. It's just permacostly."
